scenarios.text: While conducting field research, a local official offers anonymized household data without clear consent. The data could benefit your study. You decide to…

options.A: refuse the data to maintain research ethics.
options.B: use the data cautiously, assuming implied consent.
options.C: seek formal clarification and approval before proceeding.

scenarios.text: You find that baseline data used in a published evaluation may lack proper informed consent. You decide to…

options.A: leave the results unchanged to avoid disruption.
options.B: inform the team and issue corrections if necessary.
options.C: start an internal review of data handling practices.

scenarios.text: A local NGO partner criticizes your prioritization model for overlooking cultural context , saying it may reduce community engagement.. You decide to…

options.A: keep using the model for consistency.
options.B: modify the model to include their feedback.
options.C: collaborate with the NGO to redesign the framework.

scenarios.text: You’re working with an economist focused solely on quantitative models, but local partners feel excluded from decision-making. You decide to…

options.A: support the economist’s approach to maintain consistency.
options.B: advocate for integrating local perspectives into the model.
options.C: revise the model with all stakeholders.

scenarios.text: Your team develops a diagnostic prototype. A corporation offers to fast-track it for exclusive rights, which may limit access in low-income markets. You decide to …

options.A: accept the exclusive deal to ensure rapid deployment.
options.B: reject it and pursue open-access models, despite delays.
options.C: negotiate a tiered licensing model to balance both goals.

scenarios.text: The lead scientist on a high-impact innovation is considering an exclusive partnership that may limit global access. You're asked to provide input. You decide to...

options.A: support the deal to incentivize private sector investment.
options.B: advise against exclusivity due to moral considerations.
options.C: recommend a conditional agreement with access safeguards.

scenarios.text: A former colleague offers you unpublished data from their lab that could speed up your grant submission. It's not yet peer-reviewed or officially shared. You decide to...

options.A: decline and wait for official publication.
options.B: use the data with informal citation and discretion.
options.C: include the data as preliminary reference until published.

scenarios.text: You learn that a published paper in your department used AI-generated data augmentation without disclosure. It may affect reproducibility. You decide to...

options.A: ignore it since it’s already peer-reviewed.
options.B: raise the issue internally for review.
options.C: suggest a correction while reviewing next steps.

scenarios.text: Your junior team member proposes a creative but unconventional method that challenges your preferred approach. The timeline is tight. You decide to...

options.A: ask them to follow your primary method for consistency.
options.B: let them test their approach in parallel.
options.C: redesign the study to incorporate both perspectives.

scenarios.text: Two labs you support are in conflict over intellectual contribution to a collaborative paper. One claims their contribution was downplayed. You decide to...

options.A: advise them to resolve it privately to avoid delays.
options.B: facilitate a joint authorship discussion.
options.C: propose involving an independent arbiter.
